strengths: WMDD addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: distilling high-resolution datasets without expensive bi-level optimization. Combining representative feature targets with per-class BatchNorm regularization provides a practical, understandable approach.

The reported benchmark results are strong. On ImageNet-1K, Table 1 reports 38.2%, 57.6%, and 60.7% accuracy at 10, 50, and 100 images per class, exceeding the strongest listed alternatives at those budgets. Improvements also extend to Tiny ImageNet and ImageNette.

Table 4 supports a consistent benefit from feature-target matching when paired with PCBN: improvements over CE plus PCBN are 1.2, 0.8, and 1.7 percentage points across the three datasets.

The manuscript provides pseudocode, several implementation settings, and a code link. It acknowledges its dependencies on existing optimal-transport algorithms, pretrained-model inversion, and dataset-distillation pipelines, and discusses inherited dataset bias.
weaknesses: An unexplained baseline discrepancy weakens attribution of the headline improvements. At 10 images per class on ImageNet-1K, Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L, whereas Table 4 reports 35.9% for CE plus standard BN, the prior loss combination. WMDD achieves approximately 38.2%. The manuscript needs to reconcile teacher training, labeling, sample weighting, and evaluation settings across these experiments; otherwise, the contribution of the proposed components to the much larger headline gain remains uncertain.

The central formulation needs clearer positioning relative to classical quantization. With one source distribution, squared Euclidean cost, and freely optimized synthetic weights, Eq. (5) reduces to minimizing the average squared distance to the nearest synthetic feature: the k-means objective. The contribution therefore needs comparison with k-means centroids followed by the same feature inversion, PCBN, and training pipeline. The multi-distribution barycenter illustration in Figure 2 does not establish an additional advantage for this single-distribution setting.

The MMD comparison does not adequately isolate the metric. Section 5.6 acknowledges different encoder setups, while removing augmentation and FKD does not control those differences or clearly establish matched regularization. At one image per class, squared-Wasserstein quantization and linear-kernel mean matching have the same feature-space minimizer under a fixed encoder. A matched, tuned comparison is needed to explain Figure 4. Appendix B supplies standard risk bounds with unrelated constants, offering intuition rather than resolving this experimental attribution.

The solver description has consequential ambiguities. Algorithm 2 updates the weights and then reuses a transport plan computed with the previous marginals, leaving the claimed position update for the new weights unclear. Projection also permits zero weights, although the position update divides by those weights. Initialization, the weight-learning-rate schedule, and zero-mass handling are unspecified. These details should be reconciled with the actual implementation before the convergence and reproducibility claims can be assessed confidently.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the scalability claims. Table 3 compares methods only on ImageNette at one image per class, where the feature quantization target is simply a class mean. Table 5 adds Tiny ImageNet timings, but ImageNet-1K time and memory accounting, including feature extraction and labeling overhead, is missing. The reported results demonstrate feasibility more convincingly than comprehensive computational savings.

strengths: The method addresses an important practical problem: distilling large image datasets without expensive bilevel optimization. Combining representative features with per-class BatchNorm regularization is a plausible and useful design.
Reported results are strong. At 50 images per class, WMDD achieves 57.6% on ImageNet-1K versus 53.5% for the strongest listed baseline, and 59.4% on Tiny ImageNet versus 48.7% (Table 1).

weaknesses: The central formulation needs clearer positioning against classical quantization. With one source distribution, squared Euclidean transport cost, and freely optimized weights, Eqs. (5)-(6) reduce to the k-means objective: the average squared distance to the nearest representative. This equivalence is not discussed, and no k-means baseline using the same image inversion pipeline establishes the benefit of the proposed solver. This substantially limits the demonstrated originality of the barycenter contribution.

The comparison with MMD does not adequately isolate the metric. At one image per class, the optimal squared-Wasserstein representative is exactly the class feature mean, also targeted by linear-kernel MMD under the same fixed encoder. Consequently, the 0.48% versus 5.77% gap in Figure 4 requires an explanation through controlled encoder, regularization, and optimization settings; removing augmentations and FKD alone does not establish that the distance causes the improvement.

Baseline comparability is unresolved. On ImageNet-1K at 10 images per class, Table 1 reports SRe2L at 21.3%, whereas the CE-plus-standard-BN ablation reaches 35.9% in Table 4. WMDD reaches 38.1% in that ablation. The manuscript should explain this substantial discrepancy and establish whether the strongest competing methods receive comparable training and recovery settings. It materially affects attribution of the headline gains.

Algorithm 2 has concrete correctness and reproducibility gaps as written: it updates the weights and then reuses a transport plan whose marginals correspond to the previous weights. Projection also permits zero weights, although the position update divides by those weights. Handling these cases, initializing the representatives, selecting the weight-update learning rate, and incorporating sample weights into FKD are insufficiently specified. These may be repairable, but need resolution.

Appendix B supplies standard loss-discrepancy bounds for Wasserstein-1 and MMD without establishing an ordering between them. It also does not connect those bounds to the implemented squared-Wasserstein feature targets, imperfect image inversion, or training a new evaluation network. The analysis offers motivation but limited theoretical support for the claimed explanation of the empirical advantage.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the scalability claims. Table 3 compares methods only on ImageNette at one image per class. ImageNet-1K measurements accounting for teacher training, feature extraction, transport, image recovery, and relabeling would be needed to substantiate the overall computational advantage at the principal target scale.

Teacher training, recovery settings, FKD, and any retained Wasserstein-derived weights must be reconciled to establish how much improvement comes from the proposed components. This does not negate an application contribution, but the connection should be acknowledged and a centroid-inversion baseline using the same PCBN and FKD pipeline evaluated.

With the same fixed encoder and one synthetic feature per class, squared-Wasserstein matching and linear-MMD matching both target the class feature mean. Consequently, Figure 4’s large 1-IPC gap cannot establish a geometric advantage without controlling encoder training and the remaining pipeline. Appendix B’s generic discrepancy bounds do not resolve this attribution issue.

Algorithm 2 has an important optimization ambiguity: it updates the weights after solving transport, then reuses the old transport plan for the position update, although that plan generally does not satisfy the new marginals. An ImageNet-scale breakdown including teacher training, feature extraction, barycenter computation, synthesis, and relabeling would better establish total computational savings. strengths: The method addresses an important computer vision problem with a straightforward pipeline: compute representative class features, then synthesize images using feature matching and class-specific BatchNorm regularization.

The reported results are strong across three datasets and several compression budgets. At 50 images per class, WMDD achieves 59.4% on Tiny ImageNet and 57.6% on ImageNet-1K, compared with CDA's 48.7% and 53.5%, respectively (Table 1).

Cross-architecture experiments include both ResNets and vision transformers. The factorial ablation in Table 4 provides useful evidence that class-specific BatchNorm and feature matching work well together; sensitivity studies and the sliced-Wasserstein comparison add experimental breadth.

The manuscript provides pseudocode, training hyperparameters, a code link, and attribution to the underlying transport solver and distillation methods. The supplementary discussion appropriately acknowledges inherited dataset biases.
weaknesses: The central formulation needs clearer positioning relative to classical clustering. For a single input distribution, squared Euclidean cost, and freely optimized support weights, minimizing Eq. (6) over positions and weights is exactly the k-means/vector-quantization objective: minimize the average squared distance to the nearest representative. This does not preclude a useful distillation contribution, but the manuscript neither discusses this equivalence nor compares its solver against k-means targets with identical image synthesis, regularization, and cluster-mass weighting. Consequently, the distinct contribution of the Wasserstein machinery remains unclear.

The optimization algorithm has substantive ambiguities. Algorithm 2 updates weights and then reuses a transport plan computed for the previous weights; that plan generally does not satisfy the new marginal constraints. Moreover, simplex projection permits zero weights, whereas the position update divides by those weights. These issues need resolution before the stated alternating-optimization and convergence claims can be assessed. Appendix E also omits the barycenter learning rate, support initialization, and precise implementation of sample weights during FKD.

The headline comparisons do not adequately separate methodological gains from training-recipe changes. On ImageNet-1K at 10 images per class, Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L, while the CE-plus-standard-BN baseline in Table 4 reaches 35.9%, versus 38.1% for WMDD. The latter still represents a useful improvement, but the large baseline discrepancy is unexplained. Matching teacher training, recovery settings, relabeling, and student evaluation across the principal comparisons is necessary to substantiate the advertised gains.

The evidence attributing improvements specifically to the metric is insufficient. Section 5.6 acknowledges different encoder setups, and removing augmentation and FKD does not establish an otherwise matched comparison. At one image per class, the squared-Wasserstein representative is simply the class feature mean, also targeted by linear-MMD matching under the same encoder; therefore, Figure 4's 5.77% versus 0.48% difference cannot establish a geometric advantage by itself. Appendix B supplies valid generic risk-discrepancy bounds under its assumptions, but does not order their constants or connect them sufficiently to the implemented feature-space objective to explain the observed ranking.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the scalability claims. Comparative profiling in Table 3 uses only ImageNette at one image per class, where the representative reduces to a class mean. Table 5 adds Tiny ImageNet timings, but there is no comparable ImageNet-1K breakdown covering teacher training, feature extraction, transport computation, image optimization, and relabeling at larger budgets. Thus, negligible additional overhead at the principal deployment scale remains insufficiently demonstrated.

weaknesses: The headline comparisons need reconciliation with the internal controls. On ImageNet-1K at 10 images per class, Table 4's CE+BN control achieves 35.9%, whereas Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L, whose objectives are described as CE and ordinary BN. Appendix B supplies separate standard risk bounds with unquantified constants; it does not establish an ordering or directly analyze the implemented teacher-feature pipeline.

The optimizer description has consequential ambiguities. Algorithm 2 updates the weights after computing the transport plan, then reuses that plan for the position update although its column marginals correspond to the previous weights. Projection also permits zero weights, while the Newton update divides by those weights. The manuscript should specify the actual update ordering, zero-weight handling, initialization, step size, and use of learned weights during FKD before its convergence and reproducibility claims can be assessed.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the large-scale claims. Comparative runtime and memory measurements cover ImageNette at one image per class, while Table 5 covers Tiny ImageNet. ImageNet-1K runtime, memory, and the accounting of teacher training, feature extraction, transport computation, and FKD are not established. strengths: WMDD addresses an important practical problem: distilling high-resolution image datasets without differentiating through training trajectories. Combining classwise feature representatives with per-class BatchNorm regularization is a useful design.

The reported results are promising. Table 1 gives ImageNet-1K accuracies of 38.2% and 57.6% at 10 and 50 images per class, compared with the strongest listed baselines of 32.1% and 53.5%, respectively.

Experiments cover three datasets, four image budgets, and transfer to both ResNet and transformer architectures. The factorial ablation in Table 4 supports the benefit of combining feature matching with PCBN; sliced-Wasserstein and hyperparameter experiments provide additional useful evidence.

The presentation includes algorithms, training and recovery hyperparameters, attribution of established methods and datasets, and a code link. Appendix A appropriately acknowledges the possibility of inheriting source-data biases.
weaknesses: The central optimization is insufficiently distinguished from standard clustering. With one input distribution, freely optimized weights, and squared Euclidean cost, minimizing Eqs. (5)–(8) over weights and transport plans reduces to (1/n) sum_i min_j ||z_i - b_j||^2: the k-means objective. The manuscript should establish this connection and compare against k-means representatives with identical image inversion and PCBN. Without this baseline, the originality and necessity of the proposed barycenter solver remain unclear.

The magnitude of the improvement is difficult to attribute to the proposed components. At ImageNet-1K 10 IPC, Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L, whereas the CE-plus-standard-BN ablation in Table 4 already achieves 35.9%; full WMDD reaches 38.1% there. Thus, the controlled improvement is 2.2 percentage points, substantially smaller than the headline comparison. The discrepancy requires explanation and matched teacher, recovery, relabeling, and evaluation settings.

Algorithm 2 does not implement the stated alternating optimization consistently: it changes the weights and then updates positions using the transport plan computed before that change, which no longer satisfies the new marginal constraints. Additionally, Eq. (11) divides by weights that simplex projection permits to become zero. These may be repairable issues, but the implementation and claimed local-convergence behavior need reconciliation.

The Wasserstein-versus-MMD comparison does not adequately isolate the metric. Removing augmentations and FKD does not establish matched feature extractors and regularization; a tuned characteristic-kernel MMD comparison within the same pipeline is missing. Appendix B appropriately qualifies its conclusions, but its generic risk bounds do not compare the implemented methods. Its scalability argument also overlooks that, with a fixed encoder, the real–real MMD term is constant during synthetic-image optimization and can be omitted.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for the distinctive components. Appendix E omits the barycenter initialization, weight-update learning rate, handling of zero weights, and the precise use of learned sample weights during downstream FKD training.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the scalability claim. Table 3 measures ImageNette at 1 IPC, where the barycenter reduces to a class feature mean. Table 5 adds useful Tiny-ImageNet timings, but an ImageNet-1K runtime and memory breakdown is needed to substantiate negligible overhead, including feature extraction, transport computation, and relabeling.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer vision problem: scalable dataset distillation. Matching synthetic images to pretrained feature representatives, together with per-class BatchNorm regularization, provides a practical pipeline that avoids differentiating through student training.

The reported results are strong across three datasets and multiple image budgets. At 50 images per class, WMDD achieves 59.4% on Tiny ImageNet and 57.6% on ImageNet-1K, compared with CDA's 48.7% and 53.5%. Evaluation on additional ResNet and ViT architectures provides useful evidence of transfer.

Table 4 includes a useful factorial ablation of feature loss and BatchNorm regularization. With PCBN fixed, Wasserstein targets improve accuracy over cross-entropy on all three datasets. Regularization sensitivity, feature-layer comparisons, and synthetic-image visualizations provide additional evidence.

The overall pipeline is clearly presented through diagrams and pseudocode. The manuscript supplies training hyperparameters and a code link, credits the principal borrowed methods and datasets, and acknowledges that distillation can preserve source-data biases.
weaknesses: The central formulation is insufficiently distinguished from standard clustering. With one input distribution, freely optimized atom weights, and squared Euclidean cost, minimizing Eqs. (5)–(6) is exactly k-means quantization: minimizing over weights yields (1/n) sum_i min_j ||z_i-b_j||^2. This connection is neither discussed nor evaluated. A comparison using ordinary k-means feature targets with the same inversion and PCBN pipeline is essential to establish what the proposed transport machinery contributes.

The main comparisons contain a substantial unexplained baseline discrepancy. At ImageNet-1K 10 IPC, Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L, whereas the SRe2L-like CE+BN configuration in Table 4 reaches 35.9%, close to WMDD's 38.1%. Since most main-table baselines are taken from other papers, this discrepancy prevents attributing the advertised improvement to the proposed components. Matched teacher, recovery, relabeling, and student-training protocols are needed.

The evidence does not isolate the advantage of the Wasserstein metric over MMD. Section 5.6 removes augmentation and FKD but does not establish a common feature extractor and regularization protocol. For a fixed encoder at 1 IPC, squared Wasserstein distance to a single atom and linear-kernel MMD have the same mean-feature minimizer, so the near-random MMD result in Figure 4 cannot be explained by distribution geometry alone. Appendix B provides separate discrepancy bounds, without establishing a comparative advantage for the implemented pipeline.

Algorithm 2 has a consequential inconsistency: it updates the weights after computing the transport plan, then uses that old plan for the position update. Its column marginals therefore need not match the updated weights, contrary to the stated alternating optimization. Moreover, simplex projection permits zero weights while Eq. (11) divides by those weights. Recomputing the coupling or otherwise justifying the update, specifying zero-mass handling, and qualifying the convergence claim are necessary.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including barycenter initialization, the weight-update learning rate or schedule, and precisely how learned weights enter FKD training. These are new components that cannot be recovered from the cited SRe2L hyperparameters.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the scalability claims. Table 3 benchmarks ImageNette at 1 IPC, and Table 5 gives Tiny ImageNet runtimes. ImageNet-1K timing and memory measurements, with teacher training, feature extraction, barycenter computation, recovery, and relabeling costs identified, are needed to assess the claimed computational benefit.
